Stack-agnostic throughput optimization f.topic: Stack-agnostic throughput optimization for offline CPU batch inference of Qwen3.8-27B on Azure Xeon AMX (E16ds_v6/v7), including diffusion LLMs (DiffusionGemma)
Stack-agnostic throughput optimization f.summary: Baseline update: the task text's $4.56/M is out of date. Round 2 already brought the best cost down to $2.39/M on E16ds_v6 (E18) and $3.47/M on E16ds_v7 (E17), both W8A8 with 64 prompts. Per request on v6, prefill takes about 45% of the time (512/263 tok/s = 1.95 s) and decode about 55% (128/54.3 = 2.36 s). Decode at 64 sequences runs at the same speed on v6 and v7 (54.3 vs 55.2 tok/s), even though their prefill differs by 34%. So the decode step (~1.18 s, about 0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence) is limited by per-sequence work, not by DRAM bandwidth or prefill-style GEMM speed. The vLLM logs show one cause: Qwen3.8 keeps its Gated DeltaNet state in FP32 (154 MB per sequence), so 64 sequences read and write ~20 GB of state per decode step. The same FP32 state makes vLLM use an 896-token attention block. Prefix caching works per block, so the reference 512-token prompts get 0% prefix-cache hits however much of the instruction they share. Prefix caching only pays for shared prefixes of 896 tokens or more, or with the fine-grained mode, which requires MTP. Three P0 tests remain cheap and likely to pay: (1) 128–256 sequences with the KV cache sized to fit (−7 to −13%), (2) BF16 state via --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype (−4 to −8%, twice as many sequences per GiB, half the block size; needs an accuracy check), (3) a shared-prefix matrix (0% for the reference workload, −35 to −50% per request when instructions are long). MTP k=1 is already measured at +16% decode on real text (−7% blended). Workload shaping matters as much: thinking is on by default in Qwen3.8 and must be turned off, and halving output length cuts $/request by ~27% (~19% per million tokens). FP8 KV cache, FP8 compute (no AMX-FP8 before Diamond Rapids), W4A8, activation sparsity and runtime/Linux knobs are each worth about 0–5% here. Diffusion LLMs don't fit this job. DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B needs ~130–270 GFLOP per useful output token, against 54 for Qwen3.8 autoregressive decoding. Its quality is below its autoregressive sibling Gemma 4 26B-A4B, its vLLM Xeon recipe runs only 4 sequences at a time, and the literature finds autoregressive models win on throughput at large batch. If that family is tested at all, the autoregressive Gemma 4 26B-A4B (R04) is the candidate, at an estimated $0.75–1.7/M. Realistic targets: ~$1.9–2.0/M for the 512/128 reference on v6 (decode ×1.4 from batch + BF16 state + MTP), and ~$1.2–1.6/M for jobs with long shared prefixes or short outputs. WebFetch was blocked for every external host, so web claims come from search-result snippets; repository numbers come from the E16, E17 and E18 raw logs.

findings.claim: Current best measured cost is $2.39/M blended (512/128) on E16ds_v6 with vLLM 0.31 W8A8 at 64 prompts (prefill 263 tok/s, decode 54.3 out tok/s, mixed 154.1 total tok/s); E16ds_v7 gives $3.47/M on a slower instance. Per request (64 in flight): prefill 512/263=1.95 s (45%), decode 128/54.3=2.36 s (55%), measured 4.15 s. Decode at 64 sequences is identical on v6 and v7 (54.3 vs 55.2 tok/s) while prefill differs 34% and llama.cpp decode differs 13%, so the decode step is not DRAM- or GEMM-throughput-bound.
findings.relevance: Defines the baseline and shows decode (55% of time) is the bigger lever; any technique must be judged against this split.

findings.claim: Decode step time fits ~0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence (v6: 0.511 s at 16 seqs, 1.179 s at 64; v7: 0.593/0.724/1.159 s at 16/32/64). Extrapolation: ~62 out tok/s at 128 seqs (+14%), ~67 at 256 (+22%), with a ceiling of ~72 tok/s. Only ~0.3 s per step is weight streaming (~30 GB at ~90 GB/s); the ~14 ms per-sequence cost is the floor.
findings.relevance: Bounds what larger batches, MTP and weight compression can do: weight-byte reductions (W4A8) hit only the ~0.3 s fixed part, per-sequence work dominates.

findings.claim: The Gated DeltaNet SSM state is FP32. Qwen3.5/3.8 configs set mamba_ssm_dtype=float32 and vLLM reads it. The logs confirm it: 'Setting attention block size to 896 tokens to ensure that attention page size is >= mamba page size' and 'Padding mamba page size by 14.43%', which matches 48 V-heads x 128 x 128 x 4 B = 3.15 MB + 61 KB conv state per layer. That is ~154 MB per sequence over 48 layers, and ~9.9 GB of state at 64 sequences, read and written every decode step (~20 GB of traffic, ~0.2-0.3 s of the 1.18 s step). vLLM exposes --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype; Qwen guidance says quality may suffer below FP32.
findings.relevance: BF16 state would remove ~10 GB/step at 64 seqs (decode +9-16%), double sequences per KV GiB, and halve the hybrid block size (896 -> ~400-416), which changes when prefix caching can hit.

findings.claim: In vLLM, prefix caching for hybrid GDN models works at block granularity. With 896-token blocks on our CPU (528 on GPU, issue #40696), prompts or shared prefixes shorter than one block get 0% hits. In the default 'align' mamba cache mode only the checkpoint at the last block boundary before the prompt end is kept, so hits drop to 0% when that boundary falls in request-unique tokens (#45238). Partial/fine-grained hits exist (--enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache, PR #46384), but only with align mode, EAGLE/MTP speculation on the Mamba group, and a prefix-match unit smaller than the block. Some sources say GDN does not support 'all' mode; PR #36649 adds it for Qwen3.5/Qwen3Next. vLLM 0.31 CPU enables prefix caching by default (enable_prefix_caching=True in our logs).
findings.relevance: The R03 hypothesis (400 shared tokens of 512 -> 4x cheaper prefill) cannot work with defaults: our 512-token reference prompts get no hits. Prefix caching pays only for shared prefixes >= 896 tokens (or ~416 with BF16 state), or with fine-grained mode plus MTP.

findings.claim: MTP on real text (GSM8K, W8A8, 64 sequences, v6): k=1 gives +16% output tok/s at 95.9% acceptance, k=2 +14%, k=3 +6%, accuracy unchanged. With random prompts it loses 28-44%. MTP reduces KV capacity: 24 GiB holds 99,669 tokens without MTP, 70,485 with k=1, 56,388 with k=2. Known vLLM issues: CPU GDN + MTP + structured output can kill the EngineCore (#56419, fix PR #56518); MTP prefix-cache correctness on hybrid models (#47861, #53504).
findings.relevance: MTP k=1 is a measured ~-7% blended win (55% decode share x 1-1/1.16). It competes with batch size for KV memory and is a prerequisite for fine-grained hybrid prefix caching.

findings.claim: Speculative decoding at high batch: verification is compute-bound and gains shrink as batch grows. MagicDec gets speedups at batch 32-256 only for long contexts where KV reads dominate; ours are short. SuffixDecoding (Arctic Inference plugin, vLLM speculative method 'suffix') matches prompt and previous outputs with a suffix tree at ~20 us per speculated token on CPU. It adapts how far it speculates and reports 5.3x on AgenticSQL and 2.5x on SWE-Bench (6.3-7.8 accepted tokens per step) at low batch. vLLM also has 'ngram' prompt lookup.
findings.relevance: At ~14 ms per sequence per step, each verified draft token costs about a full token of GEMM plus state work. Model-free speculation pays only on copy-heavy extraction where acceptance is very high (expected 0-40% decode).

findings.claim: The KV cache is a small share of memory and traffic for this hybrid. 16 full-attention layers x 4 KV heads x 256 dims x 2 B = 64 KB/token, i.e. ~42 MB per 640-token sequence vs 154 MB of GDN state, and ~2% of decode-step traffic. vLLM's CPU backend supports only fp8_e5m2 KV (e4m3 is cast), historically not with chunked prefill or prefix caching. A vLLM RFC notes FP8 KV gives little to no memory benefit on Mamba/GDN hybrids, because the unified page size follows the state.
findings.relevance: FP8/INT8 KV-cache quantization is ~0% for our $/M; the state dtype is the memory/traffic lever, not the KV dtype.

findings.claim: No native FP8 compute on Granite or Emerald Rapids: Granite Rapids adds AMX-FP16 and AMX-COMPLEX, while AMX-FP8 and AVX10.2 arrive with Diamond Rapids (now reported for 2027). vLLM does have CPUFp8BlockScaledMMKernel, an FP8 W8A16 block-quantized GEMM via AMX BRGEMM: activations stay BF16, K-block must be 128 and N-block a multiple of 32. Qwen's official Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 is block-wise [128,128] (28.3 GB), reported near-identical to BF16. SGLang's CPU backend likewise emulates FP8 on top of BF16 AMX.
findings.relevance: FP8 cannot beat W8A8 on cost: prefill runs at BF16 AMX speed (E09 BF16 133 vs W8A8 198 tok/s), though decode bytes match INT8. It is a quality-preserving option given W8A8's measured -2.75 MMLU points (E16).

findings.claim: INT4 paths on x86 vLLM are slow for this model: compressed-tensors W4A16 is 5-8x slower in prefill and 2.3x slower in decode than W8A8 (E17/E18). vLLM's CPU W4A8 (INT4 weights, INT8 compute) is implemented for MoE experts (fused_experts_cpu INT4_W4A8), not documented for dense linear layers. torchao's DA8W4 (Int8DynamicActivationInt4WeightConfig, AMX through Inductor max-autotune, PyTorch 2.8) is reported on par with vLLM offline on Llama-3.1-8B. Because decode at 64 sequences is not weight-bandwidth-bound, halving weight bytes would help only the ~0.3 s fixed part of the step.
findings.relevance: W4A8 or per-group INT4 with INT8 compute is worth <=5% blended at batch 64, against a large engineering and quality cost. W8A8 stays the format.

findings.claim: Activation sparsity does not survive batching. TEAL's authors state speedups decrease as batch grows and their sparsity does not scale to higher batch sizes. Deja Vu's union of active MLP neurons rises from <1% at batch 1 to ~75% at batch 32. SparAMX (AMX + unstructured weight sparsity) reports 1.42x end-to-end on Llama-3-8B, mainly at low batch, and needs pruned weights.
findings.relevance: ~0% at our 64-256-sequence decode (SwiGLU, not ReLU, adds to it); not worth VM time.

findings.claim: vLLM 0.31 CPU defaults, from our logs and docs: chunked prefill on with max_num_batched_tokens=4096 (the documented offline default), prefix caching on, torch.compile mode DYNAMO_TRACE_ONCE. The AOT compile cache fails to load ('function' object has no attribute 'finalize_loading'), so each engine start recompiles (~2.5-3 min). Async scheduling is forcibly disabled on the CPU platform. The vllm-openai-cpu Dockerfile already sets LD_PRELOAD to tcmalloc and libiomp5. VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL (AMX small-batch kernels) requires BF16 weights. Docs recommend one OpenMP thread per physical core; E17 measured −51% with 16 threads.
findings.relevance: R06's tcmalloc/Intel OpenMP gains are probably already in the image (verify with one env dump). The remaining knobs (THP, larger chunk budget, compile-cache fix) are worth single-digit percent or startup time only.

findings.claim: Transparent huge pages give small, mixed effects. Phoronix on Linux 6.18 (llama.cpp CPU) found 'always' faster for text generation at batch 128 but 'madvise' faster for prompt processing. AMD's ZenDNN guide recommends madvise for LLMs; typical gains are 0-3% (~10% at best).
findings.relevance: Worth adding to a knob bundle (0-5%), not its own VM run; CPU governor and SNC aren't controllable on Azure (the VM is 1 NUMA node, turbo already active).

findings.claim: Workload shaping: Qwen3.8-27B thinks by default; chat_template_kwargs {enable_thinking: false} disables it (E16 ran that way). LLMLingua-2, a token classifier on XLM-RoBERTa-large (~0.56B), compresses prompts 2-5x with 1.6-2.9x end-to-end latency gains. XGrammar is the fastest structured-output engine, but grammar processing is CPU-side work whose cost grows with batch. On our VM it would share the 8 cores with the OpenMP threads; SMT contention already halved throughput in E17.
findings.relevance: Output tokens cost ~5x input tokens here ($6.78 vs $1.40/M on v6). Halving output cuts $/request ~27%, and leaving thinking on can multiply cost per request 3-10x.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma (Google DeepMind, 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is built on Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE (25.2B total, ~3.8B active, 128 experts with 8 active, 262k vocab). It denoises a 256-token canvas with up to 48 steps, adaptive stopping ~12-16 steps, ~15-20 tokens finalized per pass. Quality is below Gemma 4 AR: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, MMMLU 81.5 vs 86.3, GSM8K 96.3 vs 96.7, LiveCodeBench 1429 vs 1718. vLLM supports it natively; its recipe covers Xeon 6 with the vllm-openai-cpu image at --max-num-seqs 4 and mentions >=4 NUMA nodes. The cap comes from diffusion state buffers of max_seqs x canvas x vocab; Red Hat runs it as a small-canvas 'decision' classifier at max-num-seqs 8. GGUF/llama.cpp also run it. The 1,000+ tok/s figure is batch 1 on H100; sources say parallel decoding gives diminishing returns when servers batch many requests.
findings.relevance: This is the diffusion candidate the user asked about. Its strengths are latency at low batch and a small active parameter count; our goal is batch throughput on compute-bound CPUs.

findings.claim: Diffusion LMs lose on throughput at batch. 'How Efficient Are Diffusion Language Models?' finds LLaMA3-8B-Instruct 13.7x the throughput of LLaDA-8B: DLMs are compute-bound with more FLOPs per token, and their accelerations (dual cache, parallel decoding) help mainly at small batch. Fast-dLLM likewise reports AR overtaking prefix-cached dLLMs as batch grows. Our arithmetic for DiffusionGemma at ~15 passes x 256 positions x (7.6 GFLOP body + ~1.1-1.5 GFLOP logits): ~130 GFLOP per output token with a full canvas, ~270 when only 128 of 256 positions are used. That compares with 54 GFLOP for Qwen3.8-27B AR and ~7.6 for Gemma 4 26B-A4B AR. Diffusion drafters (SpecDiff-2, up to 5.5x) target the same low-batch regime.
findings.relevance: On our CPU, already compute/per-row-bound at batch 64, DiffusionGemma's decode would reach ~13-50 out tok/s against Qwen W8A8's 54. Its only advantage is MoE prefill, which the same family's autoregressive Gemma 4 26B-A4B also has, with far cheaper decode.

findings.claim: The 64-prompt benchmark runs carry ~8-9 s of fixed per-run overhead. On v6, marginal prefill between 16 and 64 prompts is 283 tok/s vs 263 measured. vllm bench throughput supports shared-prefix workloads (--random-prefix-len; the prefix_repetition dataset with prefix-len, suffix-len, num-prefixes and output-len).
findings.relevance: Long production jobs should be ~3-7% cheaper than the reported 64-prompt numbers. Prefix-caching tests need no custom client.

ideas.idea: P0-A: Larger batches at steady state. W8A8 on E16ds_v6, mixed 512/128 with num_prompts at least 4x max_num_seqs, max_num_seqs 64/128/192 (256 if memory allows), VLLM_CPU_KVCACHE_SPACE 24/40/60 GiB (each sequence of <=896 tokens takes one 896-token block in every layer, ~235 MB with FP32 state). Record a llama-bench reference on the same VM and log vLLM's KV concurrency line.
ideas.hypothesis: Decode step ~0.29 s + 13.9 ms per sequence, so out tok/s rises 54 -> ~62 at 128 (+14%) and ~67 at 256 (+22%), with prefill flat; long runs also amortize the ~9 s per-run overhead. Falsified if 128 sequences give <+5% decode, or if preemptions show the KV cache is too small.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode time per request 2.36 -> 2.07 s (128) or 1.92 s (256); per request 4.31 -> 4.02/3.87 s = -7%/-10%, about -3% more from steady state. $2.39 -> ~$2.15-2.22/M on v6 ($3.47 -> ~$3.1-3.2 on v7). Measured from the task's $4.56 reference, 16->64 prompts plus v6 have already given -48%.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h on E16ds_v6 (~$2): three 25-35 min runs plus ~15 min setup. RSS must stay below ~115 GB with 60 GiB KV, so step 64 -> 128 -> 192 and stop on OOM.
ideas.prerequisites: vllm_bench.sh needs MAX_NUM_SEQS and NUM_PROMPTS knobs; current image digest 8024248339dc. A real-text variant is needed if MTP is combined (see P1-D).

ideas.idea: P0-B: BF16 GDN state (--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16) with W8A8. Measure decode at 64 and 128 sequences and mixed 512/128, then GSM8K-200 and MMLU-400 agreement against FP32-state W8A8 (E16 scripts).
ideas.hypothesis: FP32 state is ~154 MB per sequence (~20 GB read+write per decode step at 64 sequences). BF16 halves it: decode +9-16%, hybrid block size 896 -> ~400-416 tokens (check the log line), and 2x sequences per KV GiB. Answer agreement with the FP32-state run >=97% on GSM8K and MMLU at <=1k-token contexts. Falsified if decode gains <4%, vLLM ignores the override for Qwen3.8's config, or MMLU drops >1 point.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode 2.36 -> ~2.10 s per request, blended -4% to -8%: $2.39 -> ~$2.2-2.3/M. Combined with P0-A it lets 256 sequences fit in ~30 GiB instead of ~60. The ~416-token block also enables prefix hits for 512-token prompts that share >=416 tokens (see P0-C).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h (throughput 0.5 h; quality ~25 min for GSM8K+MMLU with W8A8; setup). Risk: the CPU GDN kernel may not accept a BF16 state, and Qwen ships FP32 for a reason.
ideas.prerequisites: Confirm the flag exists in vLLM 0.31 (vllm serve --help in the container); reuse bench/quality_tasks.py.

ideas.idea: P0-C: Shared-prefix matrix with prefix caching. vllm bench throughput --dataset-name prefix_repetition (one prefix), W8A8, 128 sequences. Cases: (a) 384 shared + 128 unique, 128 out, defaults (expect 0% hits); (b) 896 shared + 384 unique, 128 out (expect a hit at the 896 boundary); (c) case (a) with MTP k=1 + --mamba-cache-mode align + --enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache + a small prefix-match unit; (d) case (a) with BF16 state (block ~416). Each against --no-enable-prefix-caching, logging the prefix-cache hit rate and spot-checking outputs for correctness.
ideas.hypothesis: With FP32 state, prefix caching only hits for shared prefixes >=896 tokens whose last block boundary falls inside the shared part. Fine-grained mode or BF16 state brings 384-416-token shared prefixes into reach. Falsified if (b) shows <50% of the predicted prefill saving, or if (c) and (d) show 0% hits.
ideas.expected_gain: (a): 0 for the reference workload. (b): per request 1280/263+2.36 = 7.23 s -> 384/263+2.36 = 3.82 s, i.e. -47%. If (c) or (d) works for 384-of-512 shared: 4.31 -> 2.85 s, i.e. -34%, $2.39 -> ~$1.58/M with cached input tokens counted. That is the biggest lever for real batch jobs with long common instructions. Padding instructions to a block boundary, e.g. with few-shot examples, costs nothing once cached.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h. Risk: fine-grained flags may postdate 0.31 or be GPU-only; hybrid prefix caching plus MTP has had correctness bugs (#47861, #53504, #57267).
ideas.prerequisites: Verify flag names in the 0.31 image. Ask the user for realistic shared-prefix and unique lengths of target jobs.

ideas.idea: P1-D: MTP k=1 combined with larger batches on real 512/128 text, e.g. 512-token news articles summarized in <=128 tokens with thinking off. Configurations: 64 and 128 sequences, MTP 0/1, KV sized for MTP's ~29% lower capacity (24 GiB holds 70,485 tokens with MTP vs 99,669 without).
ideas.hypothesis: MTP's +16% decode at 64 sequences (GSM8K, 96% acceptance) carries over to summarization/extraction text with >=85% acceptance, and stays >= +10% at 128 sequences. Falsified if gains at 128 drop below +5% (per-sequence verification cost dominates).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h; needs a real dataset downloaded on the VM (Hugging Face from the VM is fine).
ideas.prerequisites: Fix for CPU GDN+MTP+structured-output crash (#56419/#56518) if structured output will be used; P0-A results to pick KV size.

ideas.idea: P1-E: Profile one decode step at 64 sequences (W8A8, decode 32/256): torch profiler or perf plus py-spy. Attribute the ~1.18 s step to GEMMs at M=64, GDN recurrent kernel and state copies, attention, sampler (64 x 248k logits), RMSNorm/conv and Python scheduling.
ideas.hypothesis: Of the ~14 ms per-sequence cost, roughly 4-6 ms is GEMM at decode-sized M, 3-5 ms the FP32 GDN state, and 3-5 ms other work (sampler RNG over 16M logits, Python), because decode speed doesn't change with instance speed. Falsified if GEMM is >70% of the step.
ideas.expected_gain: No direct gain. It decides between kernel work (SGLang, R02/E14), state dtype (P0-B) and batch size (P0-A) for the 55% of time spent in decode. If ~4 ms of non-GEMM overhead per sequence could be removed, decode would gain ~+30%, about -15% blended.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.5 VM-h; it can run at the end of the P0-A chain.
ideas.prerequisites: perf in cloud-init (E07 used it); VLLM_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR or perf record on the EngineCore PID.

ideas.idea: P1-F: Output budget and structured-output overhead. Same 512-token real inputs with (i) free text, max_tokens 128; (ii) JSON schema via xgrammar with short keys; (iii) a terse prompt. Measure output tokens per request, wall time, and grammar overhead at 64-128 sequences. Confirm enable_thinking=false is the default in every bench script.
ideas.hypothesis: JSON or terse output halves output tokens (128 -> ~64) at equal task quality, and xgrammar adds <5% per step even though it shares cores with the OpenMP threads. Falsified if the grammar costs >10% of throughput or MTP+grammar crashes.
ideas.expected_gain: Per request 1.95 + 1.18 = 3.13 s vs 4.31 s: $/request -27%, $/M on 576 tokens -19% ($2.39 -> ~$1.93/M). Leaving thinking on (~+1000 output tokens) would cost ~5x per request.
ideas.prerequisites: A labelled extraction or classification sample to check that output-length cuts don't hurt quality.

ideas.idea: P2-G: Model-free speculation for copy-heavy extraction: vLLM 'ngram' (prompt lookup) and 'suffix' (Arctic Inference) at 64 sequences on an extraction task whose outputs quote input spans.
ideas.hypothesis: On copy-heavy outputs, suffix decoding gets >=2 accepted tokens per step and speculates adaptively, so decode gains +15-40% at 64 sequences. On free-form text the gain is ~0 or negative. Falsified if acceptance stays below ~1 token per step, or the hybrid GDN model rejects non-MTP drafters.
ideas.expected_gain: 0 to -16% blended for extraction jobs (0.55 x 0..0.29). Likely smaller than MTP on general text, and they can't be stacked.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h. Risk: arctic-inference must pip-install into the vLLM 0.31 CPU image and support it; hybrid state rollback for these methods is unverified.
ideas.prerequisites: A representative extraction dataset; pip on the VM.

ideas.idea: P2-H: Runtime knob bundle in one chain: THP=always (set before the model loads, defrag defer+madvise); --no-enable-prefix-caching when nothing is shared; max_num_batched_tokens 8192/16384; check LD_PRELOAD inside the image (tcmalloc + libiomp5); compile-cache workaround (VLLM_USE_AOT_COMPILE=0 or a matching torch) to avoid the ~2.5-3 min recompile on each start.
ideas.hypothesis: Each knob is worth 0-5% of steady-state throughput and THP is the most likely to show. The cache fix saves ~2.5-3 min of startup per engine start. Falsified if every knob stays within run-to-run noise (~2%).
ideas.expected_gain: 0 to -8% blended combined (~$2.2-2.39/M), plus ~$0.06 per engine start; matters only for many short jobs.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.7 VM-h; fits at the tail of the P0 chain.
ideas.prerequisites: --privileged container (already used); root access to /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage on the VM.

ideas.idea: P2-I: Official Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 (block 128x128) through vLLM's CPUFp8BlockScaledMMKernel (FP8 W8A16, AMX-BF16 BRGEMM) as a quality-safe alternative to community W8A8.
ideas.hypothesis: It loads on CPU, prefill runs at ~BF16 speed (~0.7x W8A8), decode at 64 sequences lands between BF16 and W8A8, and MMLU stays within 1 point of BF16 (W8A8 lost 2.75 points, p=0.035).
ideas.expected_gain: Cost goes up about 20-40% compared with W8A8 (~$2.9-3.3/M on v6), but likely BF16-level accuracy at ~25% below BF16 cost. Use it only where W8A8's MMLU-type loss is unacceptable.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h (throughput plus MMLU-400/GSM8K-200).
ideas.prerequisites: Hugging Face download on the VM; confirm the kernel exists in vLLM 0.31.

ideas.idea: P2-J: LLMLingua-2 prompt compression (xlm-roberta-large) at 2x before vLLM, on a labelled extraction or classification set.
ideas.hypothesis: 2x compression of the unique part of the prompt keeps task accuracy within 1-2 points for classification, less reliably for extraction of exact spans; compressor cost is ~1-2% of the 27B prefill.
ideas.expected_gain: Prefill 1.95 -> ~1.0 s + 0.05 s for compression, so per request -22%: $2.39 -> ~$1.86 per original-token million. It overlaps with prefix caching (compress only the unique part).
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1 VM-h; quality risk dominates.
ideas.prerequisites: pip on the VM, a labelled dataset; job owner accepts lossy inputs.

ideas.idea: P3-K: Diffusion LLM check: DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B on vLLM CPU (BF16, recipe flags, max-num-seqs 4/8/16), next to its autoregressive sibling Gemma 4 26B-A4B as the control, on 512/128 and on a short-canvas classification task.
ideas.hypothesis: DiffusionGemma's decode needs ~130-270 GFLOP per useful output token against Qwen3.8 AR's 54. On a compute-bound 8-core VM it reaches only ~13-50 out tok/s; prefill (3.8B active) runs ~460-900 tok/s. Per request 0.6-1.1 s + 2.5-9.8 s = 3.1-10.9 s against Qwen W8A8's 4.15 s, so no reliable gain at lower quality. The AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B gets the same prefill plus ~70-180 tok/s decode at 64 sequences (~1.3-3.0 s per request). Falsified if DiffusionGemma beats the AR control per request at equal batch.
ideas.expected_gain: DiffusionGemma: -25% to +160% $/request vs the current $2.39/M (likely worse), with MMLU-Pro 5 points below Gemma 4. AR control: ~$0.75-1.7/M (-30 to -70%) at a quality cost to check like E16. That gain comes from the MoE model choice (R04), not from diffusion.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~2 VM-h for both models (downloads ~50 GB BF16 each). Risks: the recipe mentions >=4 NUMA nodes and max-num-seqs<=4, and diffusion state buffers are max_seqs x 256 x 262k.
ideas.prerequisites: Hugging Face access to google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it and Gemma 4 from the VM; E16-style quality harness adapted to Gemma chat templates.

ideas.idea: P3-L: Skip unless something changes: FP8/INT8 KV cache, W4A8 or DA8W4 dense kernels (torchao/SGLang), activation sparsity (TEAL/Deja Vu/SparAMX), EAGLE-3 heads, draft models.
ideas.hypothesis: Each is <=5% at batch 64-256 on this hybrid. KV is ~2% of decode traffic and gives no memory gain under hybrid page alignment. Decode isn't weight-bound. Union sparsity at batch >=32 is >=75% dense. The built-in MTP already accepts 96%.
ideas.expected_gain: ~0 to -5% blended each, for high engineering effort or quality risk.
ideas.cost_to_test: Not recommended; 1-3 VM-h each plus porting work.
ideas.prerequisites: Re-open only if P1-E's profile shows weight streaming dominating, or if batch can't grow.

open_questions: Does the vLLM 0.31.0 CPU image (digest 8024248339dc) honor --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16 for Qwen3.8, whose config pins float32, and does the CPU GDN kernel ('GDN decode kernel: CPU') support a BF16 state?

Are --enable-mamba-fine-grained-prefix-cache / partial hybrid prefix hits (PR #46384) and 'all' mamba cache mode (PR #36649) present in 0.31.0 and supported by the CPU attention backend? Exact flag names (prefix-match unit) need checking with --help.

What makes up the ~14 ms per-sequence decode cost at 64 sequences (decode-sized INT8 GEMMs, FP32 GDN state copies, sampler RNG over 64x248k logits, Python)? Decode doesn't change with instance speed (v6 54.3 vs v7 55.2 tok/s), so a profile is needed.

What do real target jobs look like (shared instruction length, unique input length, output length, copy-heavy extraction or not)? That decides whether prefix caching (needs >=896 shared tokens by default) and suffix decoding matter.
Does Qwen3.8 keep accuracy with a BF16 recurrent state at <=2k-token contexts? Qwen ships FP32 for a reason; no published ablation was found.
Do ngram and suffix (Arctic Inference) speculative methods work with hybrid GDN models in vLLM 0.31 CPU, given they need state rollback like MTP?

Can DiffusionGemma's vLLM CPU path run on a single-NUMA 8-core VM? The Xeon 6 recipe mentions >=4 NUMA nodes and max-num-seqs 4. Its diffusion state buffers are max_seqs x 256 x 262k vocab, which in fp32 is ~17 GB at 64 sequences.
Is the 'Qwen3.8-27B-FP8' block-128 checkpoint official, and does vLLM 0.31 already include CPUFp8BlockScaledMMKernel? The docs listing came from latest/stable.

Diffusion language models (DiffusionGemm.topic: Diffusion language models (DiffusionGemma, Gemini Diffusion, LLaDA 2.x, Dream, Mercury, SDAR, Fast-dLLM, BD3-LM, Qwen-based conversions) and their engines, assessed for offline batch $/M tokens on an 8-core AMX Xeon VM
Diffusion language models (DiffusionGemm.summary: On this setup, a diffusion LM is not a credible way to lower $/M tokens. The open model the user means is DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B (Google, released 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0, one size). It is a 256-token-canvas diffusion version of the Gemma 4 26B-A4B MoE (3.8B active). It averages about 12 denoising steps per canvas, about 20 tokens per forward pass, and scores below its own autoregressive (AR) twin (MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA 73.2 vs 82.3, AIME 69.1 vs 88.3), and far below Qwen3.8-27B (GPQA 90.5). No diffusion conversion of Qwen3.8-27B or Qwen3.6-27B exists. The closest is dQwen3.5 (base models only, at most 9B: MMLU 74.6, GSM8K 75). Other open diffusion models are smaller or weaker for this job: LLaDA2.x (16B-A1.4B; 100B-A6B; 2.2-flash 103B-A13B), SDAR (Qwen3-based up to 30B-A3B), Dream 7B, Fast-dLLM v2, WeDLM-8B and RND1 (base only). Gemini Diffusion is still a waitlisted demo, and Mercury 2/2.5 are API-only. All the published speedups are measured at batch 1 on GPUs, where AR decoding is bandwidth-bound. Independent studies find AR has the highest throughput at every batch size, with the diffusion advantage shrinking as batch grows. Our own numbers say the same. From E17/E18, an AR decode step on vLLM CPU costs about 0.29–0.38 s fixed plus 12–14 ms per sequence, against 3.8–5.1 ms per prefill token. So AR spends about 3.5–4.8 prefill-equivalent positions per output token at 64 sequences (about 7–8 at 16). Diffusion LMs spend about 13 (DiffusionGemma, LLaDA2 block-32), about 6 (LLaDA2.1 speedy mode) or about 2.7–3.2 (SDAR block-4, Fast-dLLM v2). The real-text MTP runs show that extra positions per sequence per step are not cheap on this stack: with 1, 2 and 3 draft tokens, 64 sequences gained +16%, +14% and +6%, which works out to about 17 ms per extra position (4.4× a prefill token). Even a block-4 diffusion model that commits 3.6 tokens per step would therefore gain about +6% at most. My estimate for DiffusionGemma on an E16ds_v6 at the 512/128 workload is $1.1–3.9/M. That is at best equal to its AR twin, Gemma 4 26B-A4B (est. $1.1–1.6/M), with lower quality, against $2.39/M measured for Qwen3.8 W8A8. Prefill is identical work for both kinds of model and is about 45% of the wall time, and diffusion adds nothing for classification or short JSON extraction. The cheapest real test is to add DiffusionGemma to the planned R04 Gemma 4 26B-A4B vLLM CPU chain on the same VM (about 1–1.5 extra VM-hours). The bigger lesson is that the 12–14 ms per-sequence decode overhead in vLLM CPU is worth profiling. Cutting it would deliver what diffusion promises for AR decoding.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B-it (Google DeepMind, released 2026-06-10, Apache 2.0) is the only open 'Diffusion Gemma'. It is a single size: 25.2B total and 3.8B active MoE on the Gemma 4 26B-A4B backbone (30 layers, hidden 2816, 262k vocabulary, 128 experts top-8 plus a shared expert). A causal encoder prefills the prompt and later 'commits' each finished canvas into the KV cache. A bidirectional decoder denoises a 256-token canvas, reading that cache, over at most 48 steps (about 12 on average), using an entropy-bound sampler, adaptive stopping and self-conditioning. It accepts text, image and video input. Quantized checkpoints exist: RedHatAI FP8-dynamic and NVIDIA NVFP4.
findings.relevance: This is the model the user asked about. With 3.8B active parameters it needs about 7× fewer FLOPs per position than Qwen3.8-27B, but every denoising step also runs two 262k-vocabulary projections per canvas position (LM head plus self-conditioning, about 1.5 GFLOP each), on top of about 6.1 GFLOP for the body. (All pages were blocked from the sandbox; figures come from search snippets.)

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma scores below its AR twin Gemma 4 26B-A4B: MMLU-Pro 77.6 vs 82.6, GPQA Diamond 73.2 vs 82.3, AIME 2026 69.1 vs 88.3, LiveCodeBench v6 69.1 vs 77.1, Codeforces 1429 vs 1718, MMMLU 81.5 vs 86.3. Google recommends standard Gemma 4 when quality matters most. On a 686-prompt probe suite, an independent paper finds structured JSON is committed in essentially arbitrary order and task accuracy matches the AR sibling. Qwen3.8-27B scores GPQA 90.5 on Artificial Analysis (Intelligence Index 43–52 depending on reasoning effort).
findings.relevance: Switching from Qwen3.8-27B to DiffusionGemma costs about 17 GPQA points. The quality-matched comparison is its AR twin, which E16-style checks would favour.

findings.claim: DiffusionGemma's headline speed is a batch-1 GPU result: about 1,500 output tok/s on one H100 (FP8, batch 1), against 204 for Gemma 4 AR and 303 for AR plus MTP. The tech report says each step processes 256× more tokens yet is only 3.2× slower than an AR step, and that the model is compute-bound, not bandwidth-bound. vLLM recipes cap --max-num-seqs at 4 because the self-conditioning buffers are max_seqs × canvas × vocab (fp32 about 268 MB per sequence at canvas 256).
findings.relevance: The speedup depends on idle compute at batch 1. Our CPU job runs 64+ sequences and is already compute- and overhead-limited, so the premise does not carry over. The 268 MB per sequence buffer is harmless on 128 GiB, so max-num-seqs can be raised to 32–64 on CPU.

findings.claim: vLLM support: DiffusionGemma was the first diffusion LM natively supported in vLLM, built on model runner v2's ModelState and its speculative-decoding machinery. The CPU backend needed fixes. PR #59107 handles narrower canvases with sync scheduling, which is all the CPU backend runs. PR #59829 fixes async output snapshots aliasing the sampler's reused buffers on CPU, which corrupted outputs. PR #57250 (unmerged) adds a 'Jev-style' structured read: a seeded canvas with single-token answer slots, read at a step cap. On GPU it reached 8.7 req/s single and 54 req/s at 32-way concurrency, with about 90% on a language-classification set. The vLLM recipe lists Xeon 6 as a target.
findings.relevance: A test fits our existing vLLM CPU Docker workflow. Whether the 0.31.0 CPU image already contains #59107/#59829 is unverified (GitHub pages were blocked; snippets only).

findings.claim:
Other open diffusion LMs as of 2026-10:
- LLaDA 8B (MIT) and LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B (20T tokens).
- LLaDA2.0-mini (16B) and -flash (100B), Dec 2025, converted from Ling AR models. Block diffusion with block 32 reaches 2.55 tokens per forward (TPF) at threshold 0.95; 3.31 TPF at 0.85 hurts quality.
- LLaDA2.1 (Feb 2026) adds token-to-token editing. On the 100B model, TPF goes from about 3.1 (quality mode) to 5.9 (speedy mode); it reaches 892 tok/s on HumanEval+ against 240 for Qwen3-30B-A3B, at batch 1.
- LLaDA2.2-flash (Jul 2026, about 103B total / 13B active) and LLaDA2.2-mini (Sep 2026, 16B / 1.4B active).
- Dream 7B (initialized from Qwen2.5-7B).
- SDAR (JetAstra, Qwen3-based 1.7B/4B/8B/30B-A3B, blocks 4–64; SDAR-30B reaches 1.49 TPF).
- Fast-dLLM v2 (NVlabs, Qwen2.5 1.5B/7B, about 1B tokens of fine-tuning, sub-block 8, 2–3 tokens per step).
- RND1-30B-A3B base (Radical Numerics, from Qwen3-30B-A3B, 500B tokens).
- WeDLM-8B (Tencent; causal attention with prefix KV cache; about 3× over vLLM Qwen3-8B on GSM8K).
- Efficient-DLM 8B (NVIDIA, ICML 2026).
- dQwen3.5 0.8B–9B base (Sep 2026): GDN layers stay causal; the 9B scores MMLU 74.6 and GSM8K 75.0.
findings.relevance: None matches Qwen3.8-27B in quality. The only conversions of the Qwen3.5/3.6 hybrid architecture are dQwen3.5 base models up to 9B, so there is no drop-in diffusion version of our model.

findings.claim:
Closed diffusion LMs:
- Gemini Diffusion: an experimental demo since Google I/O in May 2025 (1,479 tok/s, up to 2,000 on code); secondary sources say it is still waitlisted.
- Inception Mercury: API only, no weights. Mercury 2 (2026-02-24) is sold on Azure AI Foundry at $0.25/M input and $0.75/M output serverless, or a $5/h license plus compute for dedicated deployments. It scores 21.4 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with GPQA 77%. Mercury 2.5 (2026-09-08) is listed at $0.20/$0.75 and averages 51% vs 38% for Mercury 2 on Inception's own 10-benchmark set.
- For 512/128 requests, the list price blends to $0.35/M (Mercury 2) and $0.31/M (Mercury 2.5).
- Mercury does not appear in the Azure Retail Prices API.
findings.relevance: Mercury on Azure Foundry lists at about 7× below our best self-hosted $2.39/M, but at clearly lower quality than Qwen3.8-27B. On a Visual Studio subscription with spending limits it may not be deployable, since it is a Marketplace third-party offer. It belongs with R08 (managed APIs), not the CPU track.

findings.claim:
Independent efficiency studies all point the same way:
- 'How Efficient Are DLMs?' (2510.18480): AR models have the highest throughput across prompt lengths, generation lengths and batch sizes. Block diffusion comes second and pure diffusion models are slowest. Diffusion models hit the compute roof early, and dual cache and parallel decoding help mainly at small batch. LLaMA3-8B-Instruct has 13.7× the throughput of LLaDA-8B.
- Fast-dLLM v2 shows its wins at batch 1 and 4.
- Efficient-DLM's gain shrinks by batch 32.
- Optimus (2605.24832): fixed large blocks saturate early and waste compute under load, and the best chunk size shrinks as batch grows.
- FOCUS (ICML 2026): only about 10% of block tokens are decodable per step.
- An SC26-workshop characterization (2608.23807) finds step counts unpredictable at admission time and says batching mainly amortizes dispatch overhead.
findings.relevance: Offline batch on a compute-limited CPU is exactly the regime where the literature finds diffusion loses to AR.

findings.claim:
Engines:
- dInfer (Ant Group): GPU. Over 1,100 tok/s on HumanEval with LLaDA-MoE at batch 1 on 8×H800; 10× Fast-dLLM and 2–3× vLLM Qwen2.5-3B.
- Fast-dLLM (NVlabs): GPU.
- SGLang dLLM framework: reuses chunked prefill; supports LLaDA2.x, SDAR and DiffusionGemma; CPU not verified.
- vLLM: DiffusionGemma only.
- LMDeploy/JetEngine: SDAR.
- llama.cpp llama-diffusion-cli: Dream, LLaDA, LLaDA-MoE and RND1, single sequence and CLI only. The DiffusionGemma PR #24423 has been open since 2026-06-10, and LLaDA2 is unsupported.
- diffuse-cpp: a CPU engine for LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B GGUF at batch 1. LLaDA Q4_K_M reaches 2.48 tok/s on a 24-core Xeon; Dream averages 11.6 tok/s.
- OpenVINO: only a community Dream-Coder-7B INT8 IR; no diffusion-LM pipeline found.
- Ollama: none.
findings.relevance: vLLM, with DiffusionGemma, is the only batched, AMX-capable path to a diffusion LM on our VM. Every other CPU option is batch-1 and far below our batched AR numbers.

findings.claim:
Our own calibration (E17 v7 and E18 v6, vLLM 0.31.0 W8A8, decode 32/256): an AR step costs about 375 ms (v7) or 289 ms (v6) fixed, plus 12.1–13.9 ms per sequence. A prefill token costs 5.09 ms (v7) or 3.80 ms (v6). In prefill-equivalent positions per output token, AR costs about 76 at batch 1, 7.0–8.4 at batch 16, 3.5–4.8 at batch 64 and 2.7–4.0 at batch 256. Diffusion LMs cost:
- DiffusionGemma: about 13 (12 steps × 256 positions plus a commit pass, per 256 tokens).
- LLaDA2.0 block-32: about 13.5.
- LLaDA2.1: about 11 in quality mode, about 6.4 in speedy mode.
- Fast-dLLM v2: about 3.2.
- SDAR block-4: about 2.7.
Scaled from our ~198 tok/s INT8 prefill, a dense 27B diffusion model would give 15 tok/s output DiffusionGemma-style or 74 tok/s SDAR-style if steps ran at prefill efficiency, and 6 or 31 tok/s at decode-like per-position cost. AR measured 27–36 tok/s at 16 sequences and 55 at 64.
sources: experiments/E17-vllm-scaling-mtp/README.md (decode 16/32/64: 27.0/44.2/55.2 output tok/s; prefill 196.4 tok/s at 64 prompts)
findings.relevance: This is the requested equal-batch comparison. A same-size diffusion LM beats AR only at batch ≤ ~4 (all variants) or ≤ 16 (variants needing ≤ ~7 positions per token). At 64 sequences, only small-block variants could tie, and only if their steps cost prefill-like time per position.

findings.claim: E17's real-text MTP run settles the per-position cost on this stack. GSM8K, 64 sequences, v6: 1, 2 and 3 draft tokens gave mean acceptance lengths of 1.96, 2.84 and 3.62 but throughput gains of only +16%, +14% and +6%. Step time grew from 1.34 to 2.26, 3.35 and 4.60 s as positions per sequence went from 1 to 4. Each extra position per sequence per step therefore costs about 17 ms, about 4.4× a prefill token (3.8 ms). A block-diffusion model with block 4 and an implausibly high 3.6 TPF would be bounded by the MTP-3 result (about +6%). With SDAR's measured 1.49 TPF it would run at about 0.5× AR.
findings.relevance: This is direct evidence that diffusion's premise (turning decode into cheap GEMM work) fails at batch 64 on vLLM CPU. The bottleneck is per-sequence, per-position overhead, not weight bandwidth. The same caveat applies to DFlash.

findings.claim: FLOP and cost estimate for 512/128 requests on our VM (BF16 for the Gemma arms; MoE kernel efficiency 0.5–1.0× dense, effective throughput 7.2 TFLOPS BF16 from E09). DiffusionGemma costs about 9.1 GFLOP per canvas position per step, its AR twin 7.6 GFLOP per token, and Qwen3.8-27B 54 GFLOP per token. DiffusionGemma: 512-token prefill 0.44–0.87 s plus generation 2.0–8.2 s (canvas 128–256, 12 steps), so 71–257 tok/s, $1.1–3.9/M on v6 and $1.8–6.6/M on v7. AR Gemma 4 26B-A4B at 64 sequences: 168–260 tok/s, $1.1–1.6/M on v6. Qwen3.8 W8A8 measured $2.39/M (v6) and $3.47/M (v7). Prefill is identical work for diffusion and AR and is about 45% of the wall time at 64 prompts, so diffusion can only touch the other ~55%.
findings.relevance: Even at its best, DiffusionGemma only matches its AR twin on $/M, at lower quality. Any cut against Qwen3.8 comes from the 3.8B-active MoE backbone (R04), not from diffusion. The uncertainty is wide because vLLM CPU fused-MoE efficiency and the step count for 128-token outputs are unmeasured.

findings.claim:
Task fit:
- Classification (one to a few output tokens): an AR model with max_tokens=1 and logprobs over the label tokens already decides in one pass. The Jev-style seeded canvas adds a canvas pass and gives no cost advantage.
- Extraction (long input, short JSON): prefill dominates, and diffusion does not change prefill cost.
- Secondary guides advise keeping long-input/short-output extraction on AR models. DiffusionGemma commits JSON fields in arbitrary order; a narrower canvas is available through vLLM's narrower-canvas support (PR #59107).
findings.relevance: For the reference extraction and classification jobs, diffusion targets the smaller part of the cost.

findings.claim: A block-diffusion speculative drafter exists for our exact model: z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2 (lossless; 7 draft tokens per block). vLLM support exists only in unmerged PR branches; Speculators v0.5.0 added DFlash training support, and SGLang supports DFlash. On GPUs DFlash reports over 6× lossless speedup at small batch. For Qwen3.6-27B, the acceptance length was 5.05 on HumanEval.
findings.relevance: This is the only diffusion technique that keeps Qwen3.8 quality exactly. By the E17 MTP-2/3 results (+14%/+6% at 64 sequences), 8-position verification on vLLM CPU would likely lose throughput at batch 64. It could help only at 16 or fewer sequences, or after the per-position decode overhead is fixed.

ideas.idea: Diffusion-vs-AR twin test, run as an add-on to R04 on the same VM: google/diffusiongemma-26B-A4B-it against google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, both BF16 on vLLM CPU (W8A8 for Gemma 4 too if a checkpoint exists). Workload: random 512/128 at concurrency 1, 4, 16 and 64. Raise max-num-seqs above 4: self-conditioning costs about 268 MB per sequence, so 64 sequences need about 17 GB. Run DiffusionGemma with canvas 256 and 128. Log steps per canvas from vLLM, run the 3-prompt correctness check, and run a 200-item E16 subset (GSM8K plus MMLU) for both arms. Use one vLLM W8A8 Qwen3.8 512/128 ×64 run as the per-VM reference.
ideas.hypothesis: DiffusionGemma is ≥ 3× faster than its AR twin at concurrency 1. At concurrency 64, the AR twin's blended 512/128 throughput is ≥ 1.3× DiffusionGemma's (estimates: AR 168–260 tok/s, diffusion 71–257). DiffusionGemma trails the twin by ≥ 3 points on the E16 subset. Falsified if DiffusionGemma's blended tok/s at 64 is ≥ the AR twin's with quality within 1 point.
ideas.expected_gain: Expected gain from diffusion itself: about 0 (best case parity with the AR twin). Blended cost estimates on v6: DiffusionGemma $1.1–3.9/M and AR twin $1.1–1.6/M, against $2.39/M for Qwen3.8 W8A8. Any saving (up to ~2×) comes from the MoE backbone that R04 already tests. The value of the test is a measured answer to the user's question for about $2–3 extra.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 1–1.5 extra VM-hours ($1.3–2.5) when appended to an R04 chain that already loads Gemma 4 26B-A4B; about 2.5–3.5 VM-hours ($4–6) standalone. Two downloads of about 50 GB each (about 1 min at 1 GB/s). Risks: the vLLM 0.31.0 CPU image may lack PR #59107/#59829 and need a newer nightly image or a source build (+30 min); fused-MoE on vLLM CPU for Gemma 4 is unverified; DiffusionGemma's step count for 128-token answers is unknown.
ideas.prerequisites: R04 chain design with Gemma 4 26B-A4B; check `vllm --version` and that the diffusion model runner works on CPU (smoke test on 4 prompts); HF license acceptance for google/ repos from the VM; E16 harness made model-agnostic (chat template per model, thinking off).

ideas.idea: Profile vLLM CPU decode at 64 sequences on Qwen3.8 W8A8. Use py-spy plus the torch profiler, or perf, on a 32/256 ×64 run, to find where the ~12–14 ms per sequence per step goes, against about 4–5 ms per prefill token. Candidates: fp32 GDN recurrent-state reads and writes (about 150 MB per sequence per step), paged attention, sampler and logprobs over a 248k vocabulary, Python input preparation running on the same 8 cores. Then try the obvious fixes: OMP and thread binding of the engine core, sampler settings, any CPU flags for the GDN decode kernel.
ideas.hypothesis: At 64 sequences, ≥ 50% of decode step time is non-GEMM per-sequence work. At least one cause can be cut with configuration or a small patch, giving ≥ 1.3× decode throughput at 64. Falsified if GEMM time is ≥ 70% of the step.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode is about 55% of 512/128 wall time at 64 prompts on v6. A 1.3–2× decode speedup cuts blended cost by 13–28%: $2.39 → about $1.7–2.1/M on v6. This is the gain diffusion promises, obtained without changing model or quality.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 1 VM-hour ($1.3–1.7) for profiling. Fixes may need a patched image (risk: medium; upstream vLLM CPU code changes).
ideas.prerequisites: The existing vllm_chain.sh setup; py-spy and perf installed on the VM (pip and apt work from the VM); a W8A8 model cache on /mnt/data.

ideas.idea: Managed diffusion API price point (fold into R08): check whether the Visual Studio subscription can deploy Inception Mercury 2 or 2.5 as a serverless (pay-per-token) deployment in Azure AI Foundry inside the resource group (ARM what-if). If it can, run the 200-item E16 subset and a JSON-extraction sample through it.
ideas.hypothesis: The deployment fails because it needs a subscription-level Marketplace agreement or purchase (likely on an MSDN offer with a spending limit). If it succeeds, Mercury 2.5 loses ≥ 5 points to Qwen3.8-27B on the E16 subset (AA Intelligence Index 21 for Mercury 2 vs 43–52; GPQA 77 vs 90.5).
ideas.expected_gain: List price blended for 512/128 is $0.31–0.35/M against $2.39/M self-hosted, about 7× cheaper if its quality is acceptable for the task. No gain if the deployment is blocked.
ideas.cost_to_test: Under 1 hour of agent time and under $1 of tokens; no VM. Blocker: Marketplace terms acceptance is a subscription-scope write, and the sandbox has Owner on the resource group only.
ideas.prerequisites: The R08 managed-API comparison framework; the account owner may need to accept Marketplace terms in the portal; a data-plane key for the endpoint (data-plane calls get no proxy token).

ideas.idea: DFlash2 block-diffusion speculative decoding for Qwen3.8-27B (z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2) on vLLM CPU from the open PR branch. Run real-text GSM8K at 16 and 64 sequences with num_speculative_tokens 3 and 7, compared with MTP-1.
ideas.hypothesis: At 64 sequences DFlash2 is ≤ MTP-1 (+16%), because extra verify positions cost about 17 ms each on this stack (E17 MTP-2/3: +14%/+6%). At 16 sequences it beats MTP-1 by 0–15%. Falsified if DFlash2 gives ≥ +30% over the baseline at 64 sequences.
ideas.expected_gain: About 0 at the batch sizes we use for blended 512/128 cost; at most −5–10% $/M for decode-heavy jobs at small batch.
ideas.cost_to_test: About 2 VM-hours plus a vLLM source build from a PR branch (+30–45 min, high setup risk: the drafter's non-causal attention may lack a CPU path).
ideas.prerequisites: vLLM DFlash PR merged or buildable for CPU; the P1 decode-overhead profile first. If that overhead is fixed, all multi-position methods (MTP, DFlash, block diffusion) become more attractive and this test is worth re-scoring.

ideas.idea: Small-block diffusion models (SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat block 4, LLaDA2.2-mini, Fast-dLLM v2 7B) through SGLang's dLLM framework on the Xeon CPU backend, against their AR parents (Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen2.5-7B) at concurrency 64.
ideas.hypothesis: The SGLang dLLM path doesn't run on the CPU backend without patches, or, if it runs, the diffusion arm's blended throughput is ≤ its AR parent's at 64 sequences (R of about 2.7–3.2 against about 3.5–4.8 for AR, offset by decode-like per-position overhead).
ideas.expected_gain: ≤ 1.3× on the decode share in the best case, i.e. ≤ 15% blended, for models below Qwen3.8-27B quality. Likely negative.
ideas.cost_to_test: 3–4 VM-hours, high setup risk (CPU dLLM path unverified, LMDeploy/JetEngine are GPU-only).

Hardware and Azure options: CPU VM famil.topic: Hardware and Azure options: CPU VM families, GPU reference costs and quota paths, managed per-token baselines
Hardware and Azure options: CPU VM famil.summary: Within this subscription's 20-vCPU-per-family quota, the biggest hardware saving is a cheaper size of the same CPU, not a new CPU. D16s_v6 ($0.806/h) and D16ds_v6 ($0.997/h) have the same 8 Emerald Rapids AMX cores (Xeon 8573C) as E16ds_v6 ($1.308/h) and differ only in memory (64 vs 128 GiB). The W8A8 64-prompt run peaked at 56–57 GB of memory with a 16 GiB KV cache, so it should fit in 64 GiB. That would take the measured $2.39/M down to about $1.51/M (D16s_v6 plus a P10 OS disk) or $1.83/M (D16ds_v6), a 24–37% cut, if throughput holds. The only other family that offers more compute per dollar is AMD Turin F-series. It has no SMT, so 16 vCPUs are 16 full Zen 5 cores at up to 4.5 GHz with AVX-512 VNNI/BF16 but no AMX. Its Central India list price is 35% below the US price: F16as_v7 costs $0.706/h, which is 44% cheaper than E16ds_v6 for twice the physical cores. With vLLM's in-tree Zen CPU platform (zentorch W8A8) it could plausibly reach $1.0–1.85/M, but this is unverified: there is no AMX, and the hybrid GDN kernels are untested on this CPU. Cobalt 100 (Arm) is the cheapest per core ($0.37/h for 16 cores in Central India) but has weak matrix throughput. Cobalt 200 is an early-access preview. HBv4/HBv5 already show quota 0, would need 176/368 vCPUs of quota and cost $7.20/$19.80 per hour, so they are not worth pursuing. Every GPU family has quota 0. Visual Studio/MSDN offers get no Spot, no reservations and, according to Microsoft Q&A answers, no GPU quota increases. If a pay-as-you-go subscription got GPU quota, half an RTX PRO 6000 ($2.44/h), a full one ($5.50/h) or an A100 ($3.67/h) would serve Qwen3.8-27B at an estimated $0.25–0.7/M, 3–10x cheaper than any CPU option. Managed APIs are cheaper still. Blended at 512/128 on Azure Foundry: GPT-5 nano Batch $0.06/M, gpt-4.1-nano Batch $0.08/M, GPT-6 Luna $0.18/M, Phi-4 $0.20/M, DeepSeek V4 Flash $0.18–0.25/M, gpt-oss-120b $0.24/M, GPT-5 mini Batch $0.30/M. Foundry offers no serverless Qwen3.x except a fine-tuned Qwen3-32B ($0.48/M), and third-party Qwen3.8-27B APIs cost about $0.9–1.0/M. Bottom line: self-hosting on CPU is not cost-competitive. Even after the D-series switch and a successful Turin test ($1.0–1.5/M), it costs 4–25x more than managed models of comparable quality. At Spot prices (about $0.3/M, not available on this subscription) it only comes close. It makes sense only for data control, or for a model that has no managed endpoint. Next steps: move to D-series now (P0), test Turin in Central India (P1), run near-free ARM probes for Batch, Container Apps and Azure ML GPU/Spot quota (P1), and settle the decision with a managed-API quality-per-dollar baseline (P1).

findings.claim: Derived from E18 (E16ds_v6, 64 prompts). Prefill runs at 263 tok/s x 54 GFLOP/token = 14 TOPS, about 34% of the ~42 TOPS AMX-INT8 peak (8 cores, about 2.6 GHz). Decode runs at 54.3 output tok/s, which is only about 2.9 TOPS (7% of peak) and about 23 GB/s of weight reads (0.85 steps/s x 27 GB). So batch-64 decode is limited neither by AMX nor by memory bandwidth. It is bound by vector work and overhead (GDN recurrent-state updates, attention, scheduling). In the mixed 512/128 run, decode takes about 55% of wall time. Peak AVX-512 throughput of 16 Zen 5 cores at about 4 GHz is about 2.7x that of 8 EMR cores at 3 GHz. Their VNNI INT8 peak (about 16 TOPS) is roughly the TOPS that AMX actually reaches in prefill.
findings.relevance: On these assumptions, Turin F16 may lose 0–40% in prefill and gain 1–2x in decode: mixed throughput 0.7–1.3x of E16ds_v6, so $1.0–1.85/M in Central India. HBM/bandwidth-rich hardware wouldn't help at batch 64.

Cobalt 200 (Neoverse V3, TSMC N3P, up to 128 vCPUs, 3 MB L2 per core, 192 MB L3) has been in early-access preview since Build 2026 (2026-06-02, sign-up required): D16ps_v7 $0.911, E16ps_v7 $1.196 in the US.
findings.relevance: Cobalt 100 needs at least 0.47x of D16s_v6 throughput to break even at Central India prices. That is plausible but unproven, and GDN support on aarch64 CPUs is unknown. It is low priority, and Cobalt 200 isn't readily available.

Literature on LLM inference on AMX serve.topic: Literature on LLM inference on AMX server CPUs (Sapphire/Emerald/Granite Rapids): how far our vLLM numbers are from the state of the art, and where the headroom is
Literature on LLM inference on AMX serve.summary: Per core, our best vLLM W8A8 numbers already match the best published Xeon AMX results. Prefill on E16ds_v6 runs at 263 tok/s, which is 14.4 TOPS, 1.8 TOPS per core and about 29% of the nominal INT8 peak at 3.0 GHz. KTransformers' hand-tuned AMX kernels reach about 1.2 TOPS per core INT8, roughly 20-30% of nominal. A study of real transformer GEMM shapes measured 35% of AMX peak on average. Our mixed 512/128 throughput works out to 1.05 TOPS-equivalent per core. Intel's MLPerf v6.0 Xeon 6 Llama-3.1-8B offline result is about 0.84 per core; for v6.1 Intel claims +56% from software on a 6980P system. Nominal AMX peaks overstate what the chips deliver: AMX runs at lower clocks (Xeon 600 workstation parts: 2.0 GHz all-core AMX turbo vs 3.0 GHz for non-AVX code). Our v7 prefills slower than v6 despite a 3.6 vs 3.0 GHz nominal clock, which fits that pattern, so realistic prefill headroom from kernels is only about 1.1-1.3x on v6 (up to 1.5x on v7). Decode is where the gap is. Each step has a fixed cost of about 0.29 s (27 GB of weights at about 96 GB/s, the 8-core ceiling), plus about 13.9 ms per sequence. GEMM at prefill efficiency (~3.5 ms) plus FP32 GDN state read/write (~3.2 ms) explain only half of that 13.9 ms. With in-place BF16 state and efficient M=64 GEMMs, decode could be 1.5-2x faster. Realistic combined headroom for the same model and precision is about 1.3-1.6x ($2.39 to about $1.5-1.85/M), stretch 2x. The literature's other levers (INT4 weight-only, LUT kernels, sparsity, CPU-GPU offload) help bandwidth-bound single-sequence decode or need a GPU. Larger gains still come from fewer FLOPs per token (R09/R10). Note: arxiv.org, lmsys.org, intel.com, lenovopress and github.io were all blocked from the sandbox, so every external number here comes from search snippets and none was read in its source.

findings.claim: Our measured AMX efficiency: W8A8 prefill at 64 prompts is 263 tok/s on E16ds_v6 (E18) = 263 x 54.6 GFLOP = 14.4 TOPS = 1.8 TOPS/core = 29% of 49 TOPS (8 cores x 3.0 GHz x 2048 ops/cycle); on the slow E16ds_v7 instance 196 tok/s = 10.7 TOPS = 18% of 59 TOPS at 3.6 GHz. Mixed 512/128 on v6 is 154 tok/s = 8.4 TOPS-equivalent = 1.05 TOPS/core. vLLM 0.31 logs show CPUInt8ScaledMMLinearKernel for W8A8, the CPU GDN prefill/decode kernels, max_num_batched_tokens=4096, prefix caching on with mamba 'align' mode, and fuse_norm_quant/fuse_act_quant=False.
findings.relevance: The baseline that every literature number below is compared with, normalized per core so that 128-core sockets compare fairly with our 8-core slice.

findings.claim: KTransformers (SOSP'25): its AMX-specialized, tiling-aware kernels reach up to 21.3 TFLOPS BF16 and >37 TOPS INT8/INT4 on one 4th-gen Xeon socket, 3.9x PyTorch native. They switch to AVX-512 for low-arithmetic-intensity decode. The project's DeepSeek tutorial hardware is a Xeon Gold 6454S (32 cores/socket), i.e. about 0.67 TFLOPS and 1.2 TOPS per core, roughly 20-30% of nominal AMX peak. Our 1.34-1.8 TOPS/core INT8 prefill is at or above that.
findings.relevance: The best published hand-tuned AMX LLM kernels run at about the same per-core rate as our vLLM prefill, so a better GEMM kernel would gain little in prefill. (The per-socket core count is inferred from the tutorial, not the paper.)

findings.claim: Real-world AMX GEMM efficiency is far below nominal. GEMMs taken from transformers and recommender models averaged 35.4% of AMX peak, which limits AMX's speedup over AVX-512 to 5.7-10x against 16x on paper (arXiv 2507.03522). oneMKL's AMX bf16bf16fp32 GEMM is only about 4x SGEMM on large matrices (arXiv 2609.04663). Kim et al. (IEEE CAL 2024 best paper) report about 20 TFLOPS (SPR) and 40 TFLOPS (GNR) of matmul throughput per CPU.
findings.relevance: This sets the practical prefill ceiling at about 35-50% of nominal. Our v6 is at 29% end to end, about 33% inside the GEMMs if non-GEMM work is about 12%, so kernel headroom in prefill is about 1.1-1.3x on v6.

findings.claim: AMX runs at reduced clocks. Intel's Xeon 600 (Granite Rapids-WS) frequency tables list AMX at 1.1 GHz base and 2.0 GHz all-core max turbo, against 3.0 GHz all-core non-AVX on the 86-core part. Azure documents only the non-AVX figure for Edsv7 (Xeon 6 6973P-C: 3.6 GHz all-core, 4.2 GHz max). Phoronix saw no major drop on SPR with oneDNN 3.0. On our VMs the v7 instances prefill slower than v6 (198 vs 216 tok/s at 16 prompts) despite 3.6 vs 3.0 GHz nominal, which fits a lower effective AMX clock on v7. No PMU is available in these VMs (E07 had to use cpu-clock sampling).
findings.relevance: If AMX runs at about 2.5-3.0 GHz on v7, our true efficiency there is 1.2-1.4x higher than the 18% we computed, and the remaining kernel headroom is that much smaller. It also supports preferring v6 per dollar.

findings.claim: MLPerf calibration. In v6.0 a Lenovo SR650 V4 with 2x Xeon 6787P (172 cores) produced 775.98 output tok/s on Llama-3.1-8B Offline. The CNN-DailyMail set averages about 778 input and 73 output tokens, so that is about 9,050 total tok/s x 16 GFLOP = 145 TOPS-equivalent = 0.84 TOPS/core. In v6.1 Intel reports, on the same dual Xeon 6980P MRDIMM system, +56% Offline and 2.4x Server (about 472 to 1,140 tok/s) from software alone, and says the changes are being upstreamed to PyTorch/vLLM. One snippet put 6980P Offline at about 1,956 tok/s in v6.1; that figure is unverified and its v6.0 counterpart is inconsistent.
findings.relevance: Intel's best audited Xeon 6 LLM throughput is about 0.8-1.3 TOPS-equivalent per core. Our 1.05 per core on a less prefill-heavy mix is in the same band, so our stack is near state of the art. Intel's v6.1 gains show software can still move 1.5x, but mostly on the Server (latency) scenario.

findings.claim: The SGLang CPU backend for Xeon 6, contributed by Intel's PyTorch team, claims 6-14x TTFT and 2-4x TPOT over llama.cpp, and 85% memory-bandwidth efficiency for INT8 MoE decode (1.45 TB/s effective on 2x Xeon 6980P with MRDIMM). Techniques: AMX brgemm with VNNI weight prepacking, dynamic per-token BF16-to-UINT8 quantization fused into the activation fetch, SiLU fusion, FP8 weights emulated by on-the-fly conversion to BF16, flash-style extend/decode attention, and tensor parallelism across NUMA nodes. vLLM's CPU backend vendors these kernels.
findings.relevance: Weight streaming can reach about 85% of bandwidth. Our fixed decode cost per step (0.29 s for 27 GB, about 96 GB/s) is already at the 8-core bandwidth ceiling measured in E13, so more bandwidth efficiency won't help; the decode gap is in per-sequence work.

findings.claim: Our decode cost model, derived from E17/E18 (not literature): step(B) ≈ 0.29 s + 13.9 ms x B on v6 (16 sequences: 0.511 s; 64: 1.179 s). A literature-grade per-sequence cost would be: INT8 GEMM at prefill efficiency, 54.6 GFLOP / 14.4-16 TOPS = 3.4-3.8 ms; plus FP32 GDN state read and write, 2 x 151 MB / 95 GB/s = 3.2 ms (1.6 ms in BF16); plus attention over ≤768 tokens x 64 KB/token, under 0.5 ms. That totals about 5.5-7.5 ms, so roughly half of the 13.9 ms is unexplained (candidates: state gather/scatter copies, GEMM efficiency at M=64, separate activation-quant passes, sampler/scheduler overhead).
findings.relevance: Decode is 55% of the 512/128 busy time at 64 prompts. Halving the per-sequence term speeds decode up 1.6x at 64 sequences and more at 128, which is worth about −20% on $/M. This is the largest same-model lever.

findings.claim: xFasterTransformer (Intel, arXiv 2407.07304): SlimAttention (a 1-D query-key score decomposition), INT8 KV cache with a scale per token and head, and oneCCL distributed inference. Results: Llama2-70B next-token latency 249.7 ms on 2 sockets and 87.7 ms on 8 sockets (2.85x); Llama2-7B 853.6 tok/s with INT8 KV; up to 9.9x faster first-token attention. Hardware: Xeon 8563C (Emerald Rapids).
findings.relevance: Mostly irrelevant for us. Qwen3.8 has only 16 full-attention layers and our contexts are ≤768 tokens (KV ≈ 64 KB/token), so attention and KV-cache optimizations target time we don't spend. The distributed part needs several sockets, and we are quota-capped at one 16-vCPU VM per region.

findings.claim: 'Efficient LLM Inference on CPUs' (Intel, 2023): INT4 weight-only quantization plus a custom runtime gives 20-80 ms per token for 6B-20B models on one 4th-gen Xeon socket at batch 1, roughly 40-55% of socket DRAM bandwidth. The DECA paper (MICRO'25) finds compressed (quantized/sparse) GEMMs on SPR limited by software dequantization on the vector units. A near-core decompressor would give up to 4x on those GEMMs and 1.6-2.6x faster next-token generation for Llama2-70B.
findings.relevance: Explains E17: W4A16 is 4-6x slower than W8A8 because dequantization sits in the vector units, on the critical path of every GEMM. Weight-only INT4 pays off only in bandwidth-bound single-sequence decode, not in our compute-bound batch-64 regime.

findings.claim: W4A8 (DA8W4: INT4 weights with dynamic INT8 activations, so the GEMM still runs on AMX-INT8). PyTorch 2.8/torchao added DA8W8, A16W4 and DA8W4 for Xeon via AMX/Inductor templates. The vLLM Arm blog (2026-07-29) reports W4A8 +29% throughput over W8A8 on Arm. In vLLM the INT4_W4A8 path exists for CPU MoE (fused_experts_cpu), and PR #54024 adds dense DA8W4 for AMD Zen through zentorch. We found no confirmed dense x86 AMX W4A8 linear kernel. vLLM issue #38064 reports W4A8 compressed-tensors checkpoints silently running as W4A16.
findings.relevance: W4A8 would halve the 0.29 s weight term in each decode step (about −12% decode step time at 64 sequences, −6 to −8% blended) and free RAM for bigger batches. If the dense AMX kernel is missing, it falls back to the slow W4A16 path that E17 measured.

findings.claim: The vLLM Arm CPU optimization blog (2026-07-29) shows large runtime-overhead wins outside the GEMMs: mimalloc as allocator gave 2.3x throughput, OpenMP sync with LSE atomics +9%, oneDNN dense-weight prepacking +16% throughput and −60% TPOT, a paged-attention rewrite +12%. Combined: 6.2x throughput over the Oct-2025 baseline, and W8A8 up to +88% over BF16. vLLM's x86 docs recommend TCMalloc and Intel OpenMP. VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1 (experimental) switches to SGLang's small-batch AMX kernels for linear and MoE layers but needs BF16 weights with shapes divisible by 32.
findings.relevance: A cheap knob check for our x86 image: allocator and OpenMP preloads, prefix caching (mamba 'align' mode is on although we get no hits), batched-token budget, and the SGL kernels for the quality-safe BF16 option. Some of the Arm gains are probably already present on x86.

findings.claim: The vLLM release notes as summarized by search say v0.29.0 added an AMX MLA backend and 'FP16/BF16 persisted GDN state on AMX', and v0.30.0 added a DeepSeek-V4 CPU backend with AVX-512/AMX kernels. A direct search of the v0.29.0 notes did not confirm the GDN-state item.
findings.relevance: If true, the BF16 GDN state in R13 is supported on CPU in our 0.31.0 image. It cuts the per-sequence state traffic from about 3.2 to 1.6 ms per decode step and doubles the number of sequences per GiB.

findings.claim: Unstructured sparsity and LUT kernels target bandwidth-bound low-batch decode. SparAMX (AMX plus unstructured sparsity) cuts end-to-end latency 1.42x vs PyTorch and speeds attention 1.14x. T-MAC (EuroSys'25) gives up to 4x over llama.cpp for 1-4-bit weights on edge CPUs (e.g. 71 tok/s for BitNet-3B on 8 M2-Ultra cores).
findings.relevance: Not useful for batch-64 work that is compute-bound on dense AMX tiles: sparse or LUT weights don't reduce AMX tile FLOPs, and they carry quality risk. Deprioritize.

findings.claim: CPU-GPU hybrid systems need a GPU: KTransformers (4.6-19.7x prefill, 1.25-4.1x decode over baselines with an RTX 4090), Fiddler (Mixtral-8x7B at over 333 tok/s on a single 24 GB GPU), NEO (up to 7.5x/26%/14% throughput on T4/A10G/H100 by offloading attention to the CPU). 'Challenging GPU Dominance' is about phones (iPhone 15 Pro, 1B model, 17 vs 12.8 tok/s). Sandwich (arXiv 2507.18454) separates prefill and decode execution plans for CPU serving and reports 2.01x average throughput over CPU baselines; part of the decode gain comes from using fewer cores to cut LLC contention.
findings.relevance: No GPU quota, so the hybrid systems don't apply. Sandwich's partial-core decode trick has little room on an 8-core slice. Of this group, only KTransformers' kernel ideas, already in SGLang/vLLM, carry over to our CPU-only setup.

findings.claim: Older or other characterization work: IISWC'24 (Na et al.) analyses SPR AMX/HBM inference without public per-kernel numbers we could reach. On SPR with IPEX, decode barely gets slower up to about batch 8 and gains less from AMX than prefill does: AMX speedups are 6.3-9.1x in prefill vs 2.7-5.5x in decode on Xeon Max 9468. arXiv 2406.07553 reports 18-22x tok/s from batching plus NUMA-isolated workers.
findings.relevance: Consistent with our finding that decode gains less from AMX than prefill does. Multi-worker NUMA isolation doesn't apply to one 8-core slice.

ideas.idea: Profile one decode step at 64 sequences and measure our own AMX GEMM roofline (extends R16). Run torch.profiler through vLLM's profiler hook (VLLM_TORCH_PROFILER_DIR, or vllm bench with --profile) on a decode-only 32/256 run, plus a short prefill profile. In the same container, microbenchmark vLLM's CPU INT8 scaled-mm op and a torch BF16 matmul at M in {16, 64, 128, 512, 4096} with the model's K/N shapes (5120 x QKV/MLP/out widths), 8 threads. Add a calibrated dependent-add loop to estimate the core clock under AMX load (no PMU in these VMs). Run on v6, and repeat the microbenchmark on v7 if one is up.
ideas.hypothesis: (a) INT8 GEMM accounts for ≤55% of the 13.9 ms per-sequence marginal decode cost, and GDN decode plus state copies/conv account for ≥20%. (b) INT8 GEMM efficiency at M=64 is ≤60% of that at M=4096. (c) Large-M INT8 GEMM reaches ≤40% of nominal peak. (d) v7's large-GEMM TOPS are ≤ v6's despite its higher nominal clock, i.e. AMX clocks lower on v7. If (a) is false (GEMM is ≥80% of the cost), drop the decode-kernel ideas and go straight to MoE/smaller models.
ideas.expected_gain: 0% directly. It decides how to capture the 1.3-1.6x same-model headroom ($2.39 to about $1.5-1.85/M) and whether to stop kernel/knob work.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.6 VM-h on E16ds_v6 (~$0.8), +0.3 VM-h if v7 is included. Needs a profiler hook in bench/vllm_bench.sh and a small Python microbenchmark run inside the vLLM image. Risks: torch.profiler overhead on CPU; the vLLM op names must be checked in the 0.31 image.
ideas.prerequisites: Same image digest and W8A8 checkpoint as E17/E18. Profile output compressed below the 4 KiB fetch limit (save the top-N op table as text).

ideas.idea: BF16 GDN state (R13, keep as P0): --mamba-ssm-cache-dtype bfloat16 with W8A8 at 64 and 128 sequences. First confirm in the logs that the CPU GDN decode kernel accepts it, then run an E16-style accuracy check.
ideas.hypothesis: Per-sequence decode cost drops by ≥1.5 ms (from 13.9 to ≤12.4 ms), so the 64-sequence decode step goes from 1.18 to ≤1.08 s. GSM8K/MMLU stay within ±1 point of FP32 state.
ideas.expected_gain: Decode time −8.5% at 64 sequences. Decode is 55% of busy time, so blended −4.7% ($2.39 to about $2.28/M). At 128 sequences −10% of the per-sequence term, and with the state at 77 MB per sequence instead of 154 MB, twice the sequences fit per GiB.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~1.5 VM-h including the quality check. The risk is that 0.31 ignores or rejects the dtype on CPU (vLLM's v0.29 support for BF16 GDN state on AMX is unverified).
ideas.prerequisites: The E17/E18 harness. The decode profile from the P0 idea, to confirm that state traffic is visible in the profile.

ideas.idea: Runtime knob sweep for the hybrid model on x86 (extends R21): --no-enable-prefix-caching (drops mamba 'align' state checkpointing that random/unique prompts never hit), --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 and 16384 (logs show 4096), --max-num-seqs 128. Check that tcmalloc and libiomp are loaded in the running process (/proc/<pid>/maps). Test VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1 for the BF16 configuration.
ideas.hypothesis: Disabling prefix caching and raising the token budget improve mixed 512/128 throughput at 64 prompts by 3-10%. A missing allocator preload, if found, is worth ≥10%. VLLM_CPU_SGL_KERNEL=1 improves BF16 decode by ≥10%.
ideas.expected_gain: Blended W8A8 cost −3 to −10% ($2.39 to about $2.15-2.32/M). The BF16 quality-safe option −0 to −10%.
ideas.cost_to_test: ~0.7 VM-h (three to four mixed runs at 64 prompts, ~5 min each, plus model loads).
ideas.prerequisites: None beyond the E18 harness. Run on the same VM as a reference run because instances vary by 9-25%.

ideas.idea: W4A8 (DA8W4: INT4 weights, dynamic INT8 activations on AMX) for the dense 27B. Do a desk check first: grep the vLLM 0.31 image for an x86 AMX W4A8 linear kernel (compressed-tensors W4A8-INT scheme → CPU kernel selection). Run only if it exists, with a self-made or community W4A8 checkpoint.
ideas.hypothesis: If the kernel exists, the decode intercept halves (0.29 to ~0.15 s per step), the 64-sequence decode step falls by ≥10%, and prefill stays within ±5% of W8A8. If the log shows a WNA16/W4A16 kernel selected instead, throughput collapses to E17's W4A16 level (4-6x slower), and the idea is dead.
ideas.expected_gain: Blended −6 to −8% at 64 sequences ($2.39 to about $2.2/M). More if the freed ~13 GB of RAM allows 128+ sequences.
ideas.cost_to_test: 0 VM-h for the desk check (source grep in a running image on the next VM); ~1 VM-h for the run plus an E16 quality gate (~1 VM-h).
ideas.prerequisites: A W4A8 checkpoint for Qwen3.8-27B (community repos exist for related 27B models; llm-compressor itself is blocked from the sandbox, so produce one on a VM). Confirm the kernel name in the vLLM startup log.

ideas.idea: Calibration against MLPerf as part of R10. When running the small dense model (Qwen3.5-9B) or Llama-3.1-8B W8A8 (RedHatAI), add one MLPerf-like 778-input/73-output random-token run to compare TOPS-equivalent per core with Intel's published Xeon 6 MLPerf numbers (~0.84 TOPS/core in v6.0; v6.1 claims +56%).
ideas.hypothesis: Our VM plus vLLM 0.31 reaches ≥0.9 TOPS-equivalent per core on this workload, i.e. at or above the v6.0 MLPerf Xeon level. If it is below 0.7, our image is missing upstreamed Intel optimizations and a newer vLLM or nightly should be tried.
ideas.expected_gain: 0% directly. It tells us whether a newer vLLM is worth chasing; Intel's v6.1 software delta is +56% on Offline throughput.
ideas.cost_to_test: +0.1-0.2 VM-h on top of R10.
ideas.prerequisites: R10 scheduled. Model download from Hugging Face on the VM.

ideas.idea: Skip or park the literature techniques that target bandwidth-bound single-sequence decode or need GPUs: unstructured sparsity (SparAMX), LUT low-bit kernels (T-MAC, bitnet.cpp), INT4 weight-only (Neural Speed / A16W4), CPU-GPU hybrids (KTransformers, Fiddler, NEO), partial-core decode (Sandwich), xFT SlimAttention / INT8 KV.
ideas.hypothesis: Each would change cost by ≤5% at 64+ sequences on this model (our decode is compute- and per-sequence-bound, not weight-bandwidth-bound; attention is a small share), or can't run here (no GPU quota).
ideas.expected_gain: ≤0-5%; not worth VM time.
ideas.cost_to_test: 0 (desk decision).
ideas.prerequisites: None.

open_questions: What clock does AMX actually run at on E16ds_v7 (Xeon 6 6973P-C) and E16ds_v6 (8573C) under load? There is no PMU in these VMs and Azure documents only non-AVX turbo, so all our '% of peak' figures may be understated by 1.2-1.4x.

Where does the rest of the 13.9 ms per sequence per decode step go? Does vLLM 0.31's CPU GDN decode kernel update the recurrent state in place or gather/scatter it (2x the traffic)? Is the INT8 GEMM at M=64 much less efficient than at M=4096?
Does vLLM 0.31 on CPU accept a BF16/FP16 GDN state (--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype)? A search summary of the v0.29 notes says 'FP16/BF16 persisted GDN state on AMX', but it was not confirmed.
What are the absolute MLPerf v6.0/v6.1 Llama-3.1-8B Offline tokens/s for 2x Xeon 6980P, and with what precision and software? Are Intel's v6.1 software gains (+56% Offline) already in vLLM 0.31?
Is there a dense x86 AMX W4A8 (DA8W4) linear kernel reachable from compressed-tensors checkpoints in vLLM 0.31, or would W4A8 silently fall back to the slow W4A16 path (vLLM issue #38064)?
Does prefix caching's mamba 'align' mode cost anything when no prefix hits are possible (≤768-token unique prompts, 896-token block)?
Why is the v7 instance's prefill (196-198 tok/s) below v6's (216-263 tok/s) despite the higher nominal clock: AMX frequency, instance variance, or memory/LLC differences?
